newsitem.title: USA: Top U.S. Army enlisted soldier faces sex charges.
newsitem.headline: Top U.S. Army enlisted soldier faces sex charges.

text.p: The Army on Wednesday charged its top enlisted man, Sgt. Maj. Gene McKinney, with adultery and indecent assault against four servicewomen in the latest incident in a sexual harassment scandal that has rocked the service.

The Army said a senior officer would investigate the charges, which also include obstruction of justice, involving three Army women and a female sailor to determine whether the 22-year Army veteran should face a military court martial.

McKinney, whose title is Sergeant Major of the Army, was suspended in February from his Pentagon job as the senior enlisted adviser to service leaders pending resolution of sex harassment allegations against him by former soldier Brenda Hoster in February.
He has since been assigned to the Military District of Washington.
The formal charges filed on Wednesday are the latest development in an Army sexual harassment scandal that has included charges of rape of women recruits by male drill sergeants at training bases.
The three other women who alleged that McKinney acted inappropriately with them have been questioned extensively by Army investigators.

The Army said the charges against McKinney included four counts of maltreatment of soldiers, two counts of assault, one count of adultery, two of communicating a threat and three of soliciting adultery.

In addition to the sexual harassment charges, conviction of adultery is punishable by possible jail and dismissal from the Army under the Uniform Code of Military Justice. That code also prohibits sexual relations or even social contact between troops of different rank.

Hoster, an Army veteran who retired last year, told the New York Times in an interview earlier this year that she rejected pressure from McKinney for sex in a hotel room in Hawaii a year ago. McKinney's wife was down the hall in another room at the time, Hoster said.
